nameStory: The parasitic bolete gets its name from its unique lifestyle - it's a fungal freeloader! Unlike most mushrooms that get their nutrients from decaying wood or soil, this bolete literally grows on and steals nutrients from another fungus called the common earthball. It's like finding a mushroom piggyback-riding on another mushroom!
description: The parasitic bolete is a small, uncommon mushroom that's truly one of nature's oddballs. Instead of growing from soil or wood like most fungi, it sprouts directly from the surface of round, warty earthball fungi. This bolete has the typical bolete features - a spongy pore surface instead of gills under its cap - but it's much smaller than most of its relatives, rarely getting bigger than a golf ball.

idTips.label: Host Fungus
idTips.description: Always found growing directly on or from common earthballs (Scleroderma citrinum) - round, yellowish, warty fungi that look like dirty golf balls

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Small yellowish to brownish cap, usually 1-3 inches across, with a dry, slightly velvety texture that feels soft to touch

idTips.label: Pores
idTips.description: Undersurface has tiny yellow pores instead of gills, may bruise blue when pressed or damaged

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Thin, yellowish stem that connects directly to the earthball host, often curved or growing at odd angles

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Much smaller than typical boletes, entire mushroom usually fits in your palm

idTips.label: Safety
idTips.description: Never eat wild mushrooms without expert identification - this species is rare and should be left undisturbed

habitat: Look for parasitic boletes in mixed hardwood and conifer forests throughout New England, but only where common earthballs are present. They prefer acidic soil under oaks, pines, and other trees where their earthball hosts typically grow. You'll find them in well-drained woodland areas, often on slopes or near forest edges.

seasonality.spring: Rarely seen in spring, as both the host earthballs and parasitic boletes prefer warmer weather to fruit.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for spotting these unusual fungi, especially after warm summer rains when earthballs are actively growing.
seasonality.fall: Still possible to find in early fall, but both host and parasite begin to decline as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Completely absent during winter months, with no visible signs above ground.

funFact: This mushroom is essentially a fungal vampire - it taps into its earthball host like a tiny mushroom mosquito, stealing nutrients that the earthball worked hard to gather from tree roots, making it a parasite of a parasite!
confusionNotes: The parasitic bolete is nearly impossible to confuse with other fungi because of its unique habit of growing on earthballs. If you see a small bolete growing directly from a warty, round fungus, you've found something special - no other New England bolete does this trick!
contextualKnowledge: This species has had several scientific name changes over the years, previously being called Boletus parasiticus and Xerocomus parasiticus. The name shuffling reflects ongoing research into bolete relationships and shows how our understanding of fungal family trees continues to evolve.
compareHints: Since this is the only Pseudoboletus species in our region, compare it to other small boletes in the area. Unlike other boletes that grow from soil or wood, this one exclusively grows on earthballs. Other small boletes like bay boletes or red-capped scaber stalks never show this parasitic behavior and grow independently from the ground.
